blocks.path: Asthma
s: Asthma is a common condition that affects your breathing.
It cannot currently be cured, but if it's well treated you should not have problems with symptoms.

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: The main symptoms of asthma are problems with breathing, such as:

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: wheezing

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: coughing

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: shortness of breath

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: your chest feeling tight

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: Asthma symptoms can be mild or severe.
They usually come and go.
They may be worse at night and early in the morning.

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: An asthma attack is when you have severe symptoms and it's difficult to breathe, which can be life-threatening.

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: Symptoms can be triggered by different things including exercise, high levels of air pollution, cold air, or contact with something you're allergic to, such as pollen, dust, mould or animals.

blocks.path: Asthma > Symptoms of asthma
s: Asthma usually starts in children, but it can happen at any age.

blocks.path: Asthma > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
s: you or your child have asthma symptoms

blocks.path: Asthma > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
s: you or your child have asthma and treatments are not helping, you're needing to use your inhaler more often, or you need advice about using your inhaler

blocks.path: Asthma > Non-urgent advice: See a GP if:
s: you or your child have asthma and your symptoms are not improving or are stopping you doing your usual activities or waking you up at night

blocks.path: Asthma > How to treat an asthma attack
s: If you're having an asthma attack, sit up straight, to help your breathing.
Try to stay calm.

blocks.path: Asthma > How to treat an asthma attack
s: Use your asthma reliever inhaler if you have one:

blocks.path: Asthma > How to treat an asthma attack
s: If you have a blue reliever inhaler, take 1 puff every 30 to 60 seconds until you feel better, up to a maximum of 10 puffs.
Shake the inhaler between each puff and use a spacer with the inhaler if you have one.

blocks.path: Asthma > How to treat an asthma attack
s: If you have an AIR or MART inhaler (used for both preventing and treating symptoms), take 1 puff every 1 to 3 minutes until you feel better, up to a maximum of 6 puffs.

blocks.path: Asthma > How to treat an asthma attack
s: If your personal asthma action plan has a different maximum dose for treating an asthma attack, follow the instructions in your plan.

blocks.path: Asthma > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: You or someone else is having an asthma attack and:

blocks.path: Asthma > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: start to feel worse at any time

blocks.path: Asthma > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: do not feel better after taking the maximum dose using an asthma reliever inhaler

blocks.path: Asthma > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: do not have an asthma inhaler

blocks.path: Asthma > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: If symptoms are no better after 10 minutes and an ambulance has not arrived, use an asthma inhaler again if you have one, taking up to the same maximum dose.

blocks.path: Asthma > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: Do not drive yourself to A&E.

blocks.path: Asthma > Immediate action required: Call 999 if:
s: The person you speak to at 999 will give you advice about what to do.

blocks.path: Asthma > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment if:
s: you've had an asthma attack and have recovered

blocks.path: Asthma > Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment if:
s: Even if you feel better, it's important to see a GP within 2 days to discuss your treatment and get advice to help prevent another asthma attack.

blocks.path: Asthma > How asthma is diagnosed
s: If you or your child have symptoms of asthma a GP or nurse will ask you some questions and listen to your chest.

blocks.path: Asthma > How asthma is diagnosed
s: You may need a simple breathing test to check for signs of asthma, and sometimes a blood test.

blocks.path: Asthma > How asthma is diagnosed
s: You may also be given a handheld device called a peak flow meter to use at home for a few weeks, to check how well your lungs are working.

blocks.path: Asthma > How asthma is diagnosed
s: Asthma can take some time to diagnose because the symptoms often vary over time and breathing problems can have different causes.
If it's likely you have asthma, you may be offered asthma medicines to see if they help your symptoms.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma
s: If you have asthma you'll be supported by a care team including a GP or nurse, and sometimes a specialist hospital doctor.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma
s: Your care team will explain how and when to use your medicines, how to monitor your asthma, ways to avoid triggers and reduce your symptoms, and what to do if your symptoms get worse.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma
s: This will be recorded in your asthma action plan, which you'll need to take to all your asthma appointments.
You'll be given a printed or digital copy, or both.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma
s: You should have check-ups at least once a year to see how well your treatment is working.
These will include checking that you're using your inhalers correctly and your asthma action plan is up to date.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Asthma inhalers
s: The main treatment for asthma is medicines you breathe in using an inhaler.
For most people they work well to reduce or prevent asthma symptoms.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Asthma inhalers
s: Depending on how severe your symptoms are, you may be offered either:

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Asthma inhalers
s: an inhaler to use only when you get symptoms – this is called an anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR) inhaler

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Asthma inhalers
s: an inhaler to use every day to help prevent symptoms, as well as when you get symptoms – this is called a maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) inhaler

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Asthma inhalers
s: 2 separate inhalers – a preventer inhaler to use every day to help prevent symptoms, and a blue reliever inhaler to use when you get symptoms (you should not be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own)

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Asthma inhalers > Important: Using your inhaler
s: It's important to use your inhaler correctly so that your medicine works properly.
There are different types, including dry powder inhalers, pMDIs and soft mist inhalers.
A doctor, nurse or pharmacist will show you how to use yours.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Asthma inhalers > Disposing of your inhalers
s: Return your empty, unwanted or expired inhalers to your local pharmacy.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Asthma inhalers > Disposing of your inhalers
s: When you put an inhaler in the bin, gases can leak out and contribute to climate change.
Your local pharmacy can dispose of them safely.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Other treatments for asthma
s: If inhalers are not enough to stop your symptoms, your care team may also recommend a stronger inhaler or tablets that make breathing easier, such as montelukast.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Other treatments for asthma
s: If you have severe asthma that's not controlled by inhalers and tablets, you may be offered other treatments, such as medicines that you inject, called biological therapies.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Other treatments for asthma
s: Your care team will discuss with you which treatment is right for you, including any possible side effects.

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Hospital treatment for an asthma attack
s: If you have a severe asthma attack that does not get better, you may need to be treated in hospital.
Hospital treatments may include:

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Hospital treatment for an asthma attack
s: oxygen through a mask

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Hospital treatment for an asthma attack
s: using a nebuliser to breathe in high doses of medicine

blocks.path: Asthma > Treatment for asthma > Hospital treatment for an asthma attack
s: steroid tablets or injections

blocks.path: Asthma > Things you can do to help with asthma
s: If you have asthma there are things you can do to help prevent symptoms and reduce the risk of asthma attacks.

blocks.path: Asthma > Things you can do to help with asthma > Do always have your inhaler with you use your inhalers as recommended by your care team try to avoid things that trigger your asthma symptoms, such as air pollution, smoke, pollen or animals exercise regularly – get advice from your doctor or nurse about exercising safely if exercise triggers your asthma symptoms keep to a healthy weight have vaccinations such as the flu vaccine – viruses such as flu can make asthma symptoms worse Don’t
s: do not smoke – get help to quit smoking if you need it

blocks.path: Asthma > Things you can do to help with asthma > Do always have your inhaler with you use your inhalers as recommended by your care team try to avoid things that trigger your asthma symptoms, such as air pollution, smoke, pollen or animals exercise regularly – get advice from your doctor or nurse about exercising safely if exercise triggers your asthma symptoms keep to a healthy weight have vaccinations such as the flu vaccine – viruses such as flu can make asthma symptoms worse Don’t
s: do not take medicines for other conditions without checking with a pharmacist or doctor – some medicines such as aspirin, ibuprofen and beta blockers can trigger asthma symptoms in some people

blocks.path: Asthma > How asthma affects your life
s: Asthma is often a life-long condition, although asthma in young children sometimes goes away by the time they're teenagers or adults.

blocks.path: Asthma > How asthma affects your life
s: Asthma affects everyone differently.
How it affects you depends on your symptoms, what they're triggered by, and how well your treatment works.

blocks.path: Asthma > How asthma affects your life
s: For most people, inhalers work well to prevent or reduce symptoms if they're used correctly, and asthma has only a small impact on their daily life.
But some people have more severe symptoms that are harder to control, and they need other treatment.

blocks.path: Asthma > How asthma affects your life
s: An asthma attack can be life-threatening.
But getting the right asthma treatment reduces the risk.

blocks.path: Asthma > Asthma and pregnancy
s: If you're pregnant, tell your doctor or midwife about your asthma.
It's important to manage asthma in pregnancy to keep you and your baby well.

blocks.path: Asthma > Asthma and pregnancy
s: Find out more about asthma and pregnancy

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: Asthma symptoms happen when your airways become swollen.
This makes them narrower, causing breathing problems.

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: In people who have asthma, symptoms can be triggered by different things, such as allergies, exercise, smoke, cold air or infections.

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: It's not fully understood what causes asthma.
You may be more likely to get asthma if:

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: you have allergies such as eczema, hay fever or food allergies

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: other people in your family have asthma, hay fever, eczema or allergies

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: you were born prematurely or had a low birth weight

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: you were exposed to things like high levels of air pollution or cigarette smoke as a child

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: you had illnesses as a child that affected your breathing, such as bronchiolitis or croup

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: you're overweight

blocks.path: Asthma > Causes of asthma
s: Asthma can also be caused by breathing in substances such as certain chemicals at work.

blocks.path: Asthma > Help and support for asthma
s: As well as support from your healthcare team, you may find it helpful to get support from other people with asthma, either at a local support group or online.

blocks.path: Asthma > Help and support for asthma
s: There are also national charities that can offer support and information about asthma.
